newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-British trade deficit widens in April.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-British trade deficit widens in April.

text.p: Britain's global trade deficit rose to 961 million pounds ($1.6 billion) in April, tempering the brighter picture seen in March, the Office for National Statistics (ONS) said on Wednesday. Economists had expected the deficit to fall to 625 million pounds in April, after a smaller-than-predicted 671 million trade gap in March.

Strong growth in imports in April provided further evidence of robust consumer demand and increased the likelihood that official interest rates will rise further, they said. "The erratic pattern of the deficit makes estimation of the trend difficult," the ONS said. "Bearing this in mind, the latest estimate of trend...suggests that the whole world goods deficit is broadly flat."

Close analysis of the figures showed that the overall state of trade was still fairly encouraging despite the strength of the pound, with both exports and imports at record levels. Total imports were 14.7 billion pounds, up a hefty 7.5 percent compared with March, while imports rose by 9.2 percent to stand at 15.6 billion.
"The trade situation really isn't a problem at the moment. Trade imbalances are not really evident," said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC.
But sterling's continued strength meant there were likely to be problems further down the road as British exports became more expensive.
"Sterling has been going up for the best part of a year and once it does feed through into exports, we could see quite a dramatic reversal of the recent improving trend," Coleman said.
Britain's trade with its European Union partners in April showed a deficit of 536 million pounds, far higher than the 20 million shortfall in March.
EU imports soared by 8.1 percent while exports increased by just 1.6 percent. The strength of the pound makes imports a cheap way of catering for the current consumer spending boom.
"There is a lot of strength on the EU side in imports. That is a sign of the strength of domestic demand, also of how competitive imports are at the moment," said HSBC economist Dharshini David.

The strength of imports was also responsible for the overall deterioration in the trade deficit, underlining the likelihood of further interest rate rises as the Bank of England seeks to take the heat out of the consumer sector. "This should be seen as supportive of higher interest rates to cap domestic demand," said Bank of America economist Jeremy Hawkins.

Official interest rates have gone up twice in the past two months and now stand at 6.5 percent as the authorities try to keep inflation under control. There are expectations of another 1/4 point rise next month.

Lehman Brothers economist Michael Dicks said the import data were a source of concern. "But what really worries me is the upward revisions we've seen to some of the back data on volumes -- that really leaves a nasty taste in the mouth."
The ONS revised the total trade deficit for 1996 up to 12.6 billion pounds from 12.2 billion, with imports now reported at 178.9 billion, up from 178.3.

Dicks argued that the best solution to taking the heat out of the consumer sector would be for Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown to increase taxes in his July 2 budget rather than higher interest rates.

A Reuters poll published on Tuesday suggested Brown would raise taxes by only 4.0 billion stg in his budget and that the bulk of tax increase would be aimed at the corporate rather than the private sector.

Data for May on Britain's trade deficit with countries outside the EU showed a deficit of 563 million pounds, around 30 million above forecasts and sharply up from the 425 million deficit in April. --London Newsroom +44 171 542 5109 ($ = 0.599 British Pounds)
